records.question: Which new payment and settlement technologies are live, piloted, or only proposed?
records.answer: Of the 19 payment and settlement technologies the library tracks, 8 are live in production (Continuous regulated markets; Fedwire ISO 20022 cutover; FedNow’s continuous settlement engine; Partior’s multi-bank money ledger; Systemwide Federal Reserve AI; Kinexys exports programmable bank money; NSCC 24×5 clearing; DTC tokenized entitlements), 3 are live but limited or conditional, 4 were tested only, 2 are announced or on a roadmap and 2 are proposals or guidance. 5 have fuller cards on the Fed technology, DTC and Swift pages.

records.question: What changed in the federal government recently, before and after, and on what date?
records.answer: 31 federal changes are on record, dated February 18, 2025 to October 8, 2026; 27 of them fall between September 14 and October 8, 2026. The newest are American Express joined orders (October 8, 2026); GLM review and customs suspension (October 8, 2026); First OISP penalty (October 7, 2026). 7 of them are gates still waiting on a named record (5 have not reached any stage yet). Each card gives the state before, the state after and every date on record. 18 more changes the research found but has not yet written up are on their own page.

records.question: What has our research already answered, and as of when?
records.answer: The library holds 223 saved studies, each with a one-line answer and the date its evidence runs through: 210 current and 13 archived. By that date, 56 run through October 2026, 82 run through September 2026, 38 run through August 2026 and 47 through July 2026. The oldest answer is current to July 13, 2026; the newest, “Fed Standing Repo Central Clearing Proposal,” to October 22, 2026. The biggest rooms are Banking & the Dollar (43), Crypto & Digital Money (36), Government Changes (36). An answer holds only as of its own date.

records.question: Which official government websites could the research not read, and why?
records.answer: As of September 22, 2026, the research could not fully read 30 official sources. 11 blocked or refused access (cisa.gov, congress.gov, dsca.mil, exim.gov, among others); 6 kept changing as they loaded, so no complete list could be taken; 4 could be read only in part; 2 still need the exact document or an earlier version to compare; 1 was not yet published at the cutoff; and 6 were read but could not support a conclusion. For 10 of them the monitor keeps its old place until the missing item is recovered. None of this means the agency did nothing.

records.question: What is the library waiting on, and when is it due?
records.answer: The library is waiting on 206 open questions. 98 have a date to look again: 8 are past due and 20 fall in the next two weeks. The other 108 wait for a named event, filing or ruling.

records.question: What were the White House economists arguing, and which papers matter now?
records.answer: The library saved 26 Council of Economic Advisers papers, from April 3, 2025 to July 15, 2026. 7 are flagged Immediate (Measuring Balance of Payments Deficits; Savings from Most-Favored-Nation Drug Pricing Policy; Effects of Stablecoin Yield Prohibition on Bank Lending; Estimating the Cost of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to Consumers; Artificial Intelligence and the Great Divergence; Retail Access to Alternative Investments Via Defined Contribution Plans; The Economic Benefits of Current Deregulatory Efforts), 10 are routed to a storyline and 9 are kept for reference. Nothing has been checked since July 21, 2026.

records.question: How do catastrophe bonds and reinsurance carry disaster risk?
records.answer: Alternative capital adds a funded layer to the reinsurance market. A sponsor transfers a defined risk to a special-purpose vehicle; investors fund collateral and receive a spread; a trigger can reduce principal or release collateral to the sponsor. The original insurer or public program normally remains the direct claimant-facing obligor. A hurricane, flood or earthquake is not itself the security trigger. For ordinary reinsurance the hub's rule is the same: ceded economics do not normally erase the original promise; cession ordinarily does not erase the direct insurer's policyholder obligation or prove that a recovery is due or collectible.

records.question: Who insures exporters and overseas investors against nonpayment or seizure?
records.answer: Four kinds of risk bearer, in the study's map. For exporters: a private trade-credit insurer, which insures commercial or political nonpayment within limits and conditions, and EXIM export-credit insurance, which covers a stated share of eligible foreign-receivable nonpayment. For overseas investors: DFC political-risk insurance, which covers selected inconvertibility, expropriation, violence and contract risks, and the World Bank Group's MIGA guarantee and risk-sharing facility, which covers qualifying cross-border financing and may share first loss with donor or IDA resources. Export-credit insurance protects an exporter or lender against defined nonpayment. Political-risk insurance protects a qualifying investment or financing against named government or conflict risks. Neither makes the buyer's debt disappear, guarantees a country's currency value, covers physical cargo loss by default, or authorizes a transaction prohibited by sanctions.

records.question: When does the government pay for insurance losses, and after what trigger?
records.answer: It depends on the program, and none pays without its own trigger record. TRIP: federal share after a certified act, insurer deductible and program trigger under statute. NFIP: federal primary flood-insurance program with contractors, reinsurance and borrowing. State catastrophe fund: statutory wholesale reimbursement layer. Guaranty association: limited post-impairment or insolvency protection. PBGC: federal limited guarantee for covered private defined-benefit pensions. An FHLBank advance is a secured liquidity loan from a government-chartered member-owned bank. Program authority and available capacity are not a paid federal claim.

records.question: What happens to your policy if your insurer fails?
records.answer: A domestic insurer does not ordinarily enter the same federal bankruptcy process as an industrial company. State insurance law, the domiciliary commissioner and a supervising state court instead control conservation, rehabilitation or liquidation. Liquidation normally triggers the guaranty duty; financial distress alone does not. Coverage, limits, residency and product eligibility are state-law questions. The guaranty system does not make every creditor whole, insure the insurer, or convert failure into a federal bailout.
